intro: Read the deck for the law, dates and figures, and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, gives you something to remember and warns you where practice slips. Work the section exercises in pencil, answer the recall questions before you check, and verify any legal position against a current judgment before you rely on it.

sections.title: Why caste belongs in development practice
sections.big_idea: Caste is a structure that allocates land, work and respect by birth. **Ask who is in the data, who controls access and who benefits**, measured separately.
in_plain_words: Treating caste as culture leaves a programme neutral and puts uneven uptake down to awareness. Treating it as structure asks who is excluded, by whom and through which institution. Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes made up about a quarter of India's population in 2011, and OBCs have had no Census count since 1931.

Poverty targeting alone misses caste, because Dalit graduates with equal qualifications get fewer interview calls. Three questions travel with you: who is in the data and who is missing, who controls the access point, and who benefits when measured separately. Use legal categories for legal meaning and self-chosen names for people, and never write a person's caste into a report without consent.

left.title: Caste as culture
items: Uptake gaps put down to awareness

right.title: Caste as structure
items: Asks who is excluded, and by whom
Designs delivery and data around it

Communities notified under Article 342; many prefer Adivasi.
Socially and educationally backward classes; central and state lists differ.

worked_example.title: Size the legal categories, then spot who is missing
worked_example.setup: Use the 2011 Census figures: SCs 201.4 million (16.6%) and STs 104.3 million (8.6%). A household survey also lists hamlets from the panchayat office.
steps: Combined share = 16.6 + 8.6 = 25.2 per cent, about a quarter of the population.
Combined people = 201.4 + 104.3 = 305.7 million.
Question 1, who is in the data: the panchayat's hamlet list may omit the Dalit basti on the edge of the village.
Fix it by mapping hamlets with residents before sampling.
worked_example.answer: About a quarter of the population, or 305.7 million people, and the survey needs a resident-drawn hamlet map.

mistakes: Treating caste as background culture. The programme then misreads uptake gaps as awareness gaps.
Relying on poverty targeting alone. The evidence shows caste affects people at every income level.
Quoting the SC and ST count as the whole story. OBCs have had no Census count since 1931.
Writing a person's caste into a report without consent, or using caste names as insults.

recall.q: What share of India's population were SCs and STs in 2011?
recall.a: About a quarter: 16.6% and 8.6%.

recall.q: State the three questions to bring to any programme.
recall.a: Who is in the data and who is missing; who controls the access point; who benefits, measured separately.

recall.q: Which article notifies Scheduled Castes?
recall.a: Article 341.

recall.q: When was the last Census count of OBCs?
What does the caste-aware lens add to the poverty-only lens?
recall.a: Assets, networks, occupational segregation, violence and dignity, with every outcome disaggregated by caste.

sections.title: Varna, jati and how caste works
sections.big_idea: Varna is a textbook scheme and jati is the group people live in. **Endogamy reproduces the jati**, and untouchability is its extreme form.
in_plain_words: Varna is a four-part scheme in Brahmanical texts, while jati is the endogamous birth group, numbering in the thousands and specific to a region. With 1,241 notified SC groups in 2011, no four-part scheme can describe the field, so researchers work with jati. Ambedkar argued in 1916 that endogamy is caste's defining feature.

A jati system works through endogamy, hierarchy, hereditary occupation, purity and pollution, and spatial segregation. The IHDS-II test found 27% of households practising untouchability, and 52% among Brahmin respondents. Practice varies by state, and 15% of SC and 22% of ST respondents admitted it, because inequality is graded. Caste changes form: occupation rules weakened while endogamy and land concentration persisted.

key_terms.meaning: A fourfold scheme of ranked social order, written down by priests.
The endogamous birth group people actually belong to; regional and numbering thousands.
Marriage only within the group; the mechanism that reproduces it.
Treating some castes as ritually polluting; an offence under the PCR Act 1955.
Each group is subordinated to those above and placed above others below.

worked_example.title: Name the feature
worked_example.setup: A field team lists four things it saw. Name the jati feature behind each.
steps: Separate cups at a health centre: purity and pollution.
A tap placed in the main village only: spatial segregation.
Sanitation work concentrated among Dalit castes: hereditary occupation.
Dowry and honour violence against inter-caste couples: endogamy.
worked_example.answer: Purity and pollution, spatial segregation, hereditary occupation and endogamy.

mistakes: Mixing up varna and jati. Most inequality a practitioner meets operates through jati.
Saying caste is disappearing without naming the feature. Occupation rules weakened, while endogamy persisted.
Reading an average untouchability rate for every state. It was highest in the Hindi-speaking north and centre, lowest in West Bengal and Kerala.
Treating a Dalit beneficiary group as homogeneous, when graded inequality runs inside it.

recall.q: Which scholar named endogamy as caste's defining feature, and when?
recall.a: B. R. Ambedkar, in 1916.

recall.q: How many groups were notified as SCs in the 2011 Census?
What did the IHDS-II two-question test find?
recall.a: 27% of households practised untouchability, 52% among Brahmin respondents and 33% among OBC.

recall.q: Why might self-reports understate untouchability?
recall.a: Admitting it means admitting an offence under the PCR Act 1955.

recall.q: What is graded inequality?
recall.a: Each group is subordinated to those above and placed above others below.

sections.title: Histories: census, colony and scholarship
sections.big_idea: Every caste category in current data has a history. **Record the list version you used**, and expect classification to be contested.
in_plain_words: Colonial censuses from 1871 recorded caste, and the 1901 census under Risley tried to rank every caste, which prompted groups to petition for higher names. Dirks argues colonial rule made caste the master category, and critics say this can underplay precolonial untouchability. Both points hold.

Srinivas supplied sanskritisation, which is mobility within the hierarchy, and the dominant caste, which is numerically strong and holds land and power. The Poona Pact of 24 September 1932 replaced separate electorates with reserved seats. For practice: record list versions, expect contested classification, avoid national rankings, remember that counting changes behaviour, and let people self-identify.

events.what: Many local hierarchies, varying by region
Constitution creates SC and ST lists
Caste enumeration returns to the Census

diagram.caption: how caste became an administrative category

key_terms.meaning: The colonial label from which the lists of Scheduled Castes descend.
A lower-ranked group adopts higher-caste practices to claim status; the hierarchy is unchanged.
Numerically strong locally, with preponderant economic and political power through land.
Only a group member may stand, but everyone in the constituency votes.
Asking people their caste; better than inferring from surnames.

worked_example.title: Put the events in order
worked_example.setup: A colleague gives you five labels: Poona Pact, Constitution creates SC and ST lists, Risley's ranking attempt, census returns caste enumeration, colonial censuses begin. Order them.
steps: Colonial censuses recording caste for every household begin in 1871.
The 1901 census attempts a national ranking of castes.
The Poona Pact of 24 September 1932 replaces separate electorates with reserved seats.
The 1950 Constitution creates the SC and ST lists.
Caste enumeration returns to the Census in 2027.

mistakes: Treating caste as invented by colonial rule. The deck holds that caste predates it, and colonial rule changed how it was recorded.
Using one national ranking. A jati can be dominant in one district and marginal in another.
Inferring caste from surnames, which is error-prone and can be harmful.
Forgetting that SC, ST and OBC lists change by order and Act, so trends can reflect list changes.

recall.q: What did Risley's 1901 census attempt?
recall.a: To classify Hindu castes under the four varnas and rank them by social precedence.

recall.q: What does Dirks argue in Castes of Mind?
recall.a: Colonial rule remade caste: census-taking, ethnography and law made it the master category.

recall.q: Define sanskritisation.
recall.a: A lower-ranked group adopts higher-caste practices to claim higher status, without changing the hierarchy.

recall.q: What did the Poona Pact replace?
recall.a: Separate electorates, with seats reserved in a joint electorate.

recall.q: Name two of the five lessons for practitioners.
recall.a: Any two of: categories are made; classification is political; local rank varies; counting changes behaviour; self-identification beats imputation.

sections.title: Phule, Ambedkar and the anti-caste tradition
sections.big_idea: Phule and Ambedkar give practitioners four mechanisms to look for: **endogamy, assigned occupation, graded inequality and religious sanction**.
in_plain_words: Jotirao Phule (1827–1890) built the first sustained modern movement against caste: a school for lower-caste girls in 1848 with Savitribai teaching, then Gulamgiri and the Satyashodhak Samaj in 1873. The Phules also showed that caste and gender cannot be separated, since control over women's marriage and sexuality enforces endogamy.

Ambedkar's dates anchor the section: 1916 endogamy, 1927 Mahad, 1932 Poona Pact, 1936 Annihilation of Caste, 1956 conversion. His argument that caste is a graded division of labourers, fixed by birth, is labour economics, and his ideal is liberty, equality and fraternity. The wider tradition includes Narayana Guru, Periyar and Kanshi Ram.

events.what: Phule school for lower-caste girls opens

key_terms.meaning: Society of Truth Seekers, founded by Phule in 1873.
The 1936 speech Ambedkar published himself after it was never delivered.
Ambedkar's term for caste: graded and fixed by birth, unlike division of labour.
Many shared interests, free contact between groups and a habit of respect.
The 1927 claim to drink from the public Chavdar tank.

worked_example.title: Match mechanism to response
worked_example.setup: Ambedkar's analysis gives four mechanisms. Pair each with the observable sign and a programme response from the deck.
steps: Endogamy: inter-caste couples face violence, so offer safe-space services, legal aid and support for couples.
Occupational assignment: Dalit castes are over-represented in sanitation and leather, so offer skills and capital for exit, mechanisation and dignity at work.
Graded inequality: benefits are captured by better-off sub-groups, so disaggregate and target within SC and ST categories.
Religious sanction: exclusion is justified by custom, so build rights awareness grounded in Article 17.
worked_example.answer: Four mechanisms, each with an observable sign and a programme response.

mistakes: Reading Ambedkar as only a legal figure. His writing combines anthropology, economics and law.
Treating inter-marriage as his whole answer. He argued the real remedy also involved destroying belief in the sanctity of the Shastras.
Forcing mixed-caste contact without protection, which can expose Dalit participants to backlash.
Quoting these figures from memory. Go to a published edition.

recall.q: When did Phule and Savitribai open the school for lower-caste girls?
What did Ambedkar identify as the mechanism of caste in 1916?
recall.a: Endogamy.

recall.q: Which three dates mark Ambedkar's 1927, 1932 and 1936 acts?
recall.a: Mahad Satyagraha, Poona Pact, and Annihilation of Caste.

recall.q: What was the Jat-Pat-Todak Mandal's reaction to the printed address?
recall.a: They asked him to cut it, he refused, and the conference was cancelled.

recall.q: Name two figures from the wider anti-caste tradition.
recall.a: Any two of Narayana Guru, Periyar, Kanshi Ram.

sections.title: Untouchability and the criminal law
sections.big_idea: Article 17 abolishes untouchability, and two statutes enforce it. **The record of a case shows whether the law works**: dates, sections and compensation.
in_plain_words: Article 17 forbids untouchability in any form. The PCR Act 1955 covers access offences such as entry to places of worship, shops and hospitals. The PoA Act 1989 targets violence by a person outside the SC and ST communities, widened by the 2015 amendment with new offences, Special Courts and victim rights. Section 18A (2018) reversed the Mahajan safeguards.

Manual scavenging is caste as occupation written into law: the 2013 Act replaced a 1993 Act, and 58,098 manual scavengers were identified in the 2013 and 2018 surveys. Deaths in sewers and septic tanks continue. Between an incident and a conviction there are five weak points, each a place for paralegals to help, and the SC and ST commissions can move a stalled case.

diagram.caption: where the law on paper and in practice diverge

key_terms.meaning: Abolishes untouchability and makes enforcing any disability from it an offence.
Access offences: places of worship, shops, hospitals, schools and services.
Atrocities by non-SC and non-ST persons against SC or ST persons.
2018 insertion removing preliminary inquiry, arrest approval and anticipatory bail.
Cleaning human excreta by hand; the clearest surviving case of caste-assigned work.

worked_example.title: Read two numbers on manual scavenging
worked_example.setup: The deck gives 58,098 manual scavengers identified, 32,473 of them in Uttar Pradesh, and compensation for a sewer death raised from Rs 10 lakh to Rs 30 lakh.
steps: Uttar Pradesh share = 32,473 ÷ 58,098 = 0.559, or about 56%, so more than half.
Compensation increase = 30 ÷ 10 = 3 times.
Both figures come from named sources: a Lok Sabha reply and Balram Singh v Union of India.
Check which definition a death figure uses, since the government separates manual scavenging from hazardous sewer cleaning.
worked_example.answer: About 56% of identified manual scavengers are in Uttar Pradesh, and compensation tripled.

mistakes: Confusing the two statutes. The PCR Act covers access offences, and the PoA Act covers atrocities.
Expecting strong statutes to enforce themselves. The deck names five weak points between an incident and a conviction.
Quoting a death figure without the definition. Manual scavenging and hazardous cleaning are counted separately.
Keeping no case record. Date of complaint, FIR, sections applied and compensation show whether the law works.

recall.q: What does Article 17 do?
recall.a: Abolishes untouchability, forbids its practice and makes enforcing any disability from it an offence.

recall.q: Name two changes made by the 2015 amendment.
recall.a: Any two of new offences, exclusive Special Courts, victim and witness rights, a two-month trial target, presumed knowledge of caste.

recall.q: What did Section 18A reverse?
recall.a: The preliminary inquiry, the approval for arrest and the bar on anticipatory bail from the Mahajan ruling.

recall.q: How much is compensation for a sewer death?
recall.a: Rs 30 lakh, raised from Rs 10 lakh.

recall.q: Name the constitutional article for the SC and ST commissions.
recall.a: Article 338 for SCs and 338A for STs.

sections.title: The Constitution and reservations
sections.big_idea: Reservation rests on special provisions and the **Indra Sawhney framework**. SC sub-classification is permitted, and a creamy layer for SCs and STs is not decided.
in_plain_words: Articles 15 and 16 permit special provisions, and Articles 341 and 342 decide who is SC or ST by state lists. Central direct recruitment reserves 15% for SCs, 7.5% for STs, 27% for OBCs and 10% for EWS, which reaches 59.5%. Mandal (1980) and Indra Sawhney (1992) set the 27%, the creamy layer and the 50% ceiling.

Janhit Abhiyan (2022) upheld EWS by three votes to two. Davinder Singh (2024) held six to one that states may sub-classify SCs on quantifiable data, and four judges' views on a creamy layer are outside the order. Political reservation under Articles 330 and 332 changes policy and runs to January 2030 unless extended. The 102nd and 105th Amendments settled OBC lists.

key_terms.meaning: Advanced members of a backward class excluded above an income and status test.
Dividing the SC quota for the most under-represented SC groups; permitted by Davinder Singh.
Economically weaker sections outside SC, ST and OBC; up to 10% under Article 16(6).
Indra Sawhney's limit, save in extraordinary situations.
Presidential notification of Scheduled Castes by state.

worked_example.title: Add up the central quotas
worked_example.setup: For direct recruitment by open competition, the deck gives 15% SC, 7.5% ST, 27% OBC and 10% EWS.
steps: SC and ST together = 15 + 7.5 = 22.5.
Add OBC: 22.5 + 27 = 49.5, which stays below half.
The deck states that with EWS central reservation in direct recruitment reaches 59.5%.

mistakes: Reporting a creamy layer for SCs and STs as law. It is a view of four judges that the Union has rejected, as of October 2026.
Treating the separate opinions in Davinder Singh as its holding. Sub-classification is the holding.
Recording OBC status without saying central or state list.
Advising on a promotion roster from a summary instead of the latest judgment.

recall.q: What did Indra Sawhney (1992) set for the ceiling?
recall.a: Reservation should not exceed half of posts, save in extraordinary situations.

recall.q: How did Janhit Abhiyan (2022) come out?
recall.a: The EWS amendment was upheld by three votes to two.

recall.q: What did Davinder Singh (2024) overrule?
recall.a: E. V. Chinnaiah (2005), allowing states to sub-classify SCs.

recall.q: How many Lok Sabha seats are reserved for SCs and STs?
recall.a: 84 for SCs and 47 for STs.

recall.q: Which amendment restored the states' power over OBC lists?
recall.a: The 105th Amendment, August 2021.

sections.title: Caste in the economy
sections.big_idea: Caste operates in land, markets, hiring, enterprise and schooling. **Studies hold everything else constant** to show the gap is caste.
in_plain_words: Land is the oldest caste asset: SECC 2011 found 29.97% of rural households landless and dependent on manual casual labour. Anderson (2011) found low-caste households earned more where a low caste dominated, because water trade breaks down across castes. Thorat and Attewell found a Dalit applicant's odds of an interview call were about two-thirds of a high-caste Hindu's.

Correspondence studies persuade because only the signal varies, though they test one hiring stage and raise consent questions. Iyer, Khanna and Varshney show SCs and STs own far fewer enterprises than their share. Munshi and Rosenzweig show networks help and trap. Hoff and Pandey show that announcing caste opens a performance gap.

key_terms.meaning: Matched applications differing only in a caste or religion signal.
Social capital that finds jobs and lends money, and also steers into traditional work.
Released 3 July 2015; found 29.97% of rural households landless.
Hoff and Pandey's reading of why low-caste performance fell when caste was announced.
An interview call; the outcome measured by the hiring study.

worked_example.title: Two sample sizes
worked_example.setup: Thorat and Attewell sent 4,808 applications to 548 advertisements. Hoff and Pandey used 321 high-caste and 321 low-caste boys.
steps: Applications per advertisement = 4,808 ÷ 548 = 8.77, so about nine applications to each.
Boys in the experiment = 321 + 321 = 642.
Hoff and Pandey found no caste gap when caste was hidden, and a large gap when it was announced.
Both designs vary the signal and hold everything else constant.
worked_example.answer: About nine applications per advertisement, and 642 boys.

mistakes: Reading survey gaps as proof of discrimination. Surveys cannot separate discrimination from schooling or skills.
Assuming an open local market. In a village dominated by another caste, trade can break down.
Treating the hiring result as the whole labour market. It covers only the first stage.
Naming caste publicly in a classroom or training, which can lower performance.

recall.q: What did SECC 2011 find on rural landlessness?
recall.a: 29.97% of rural households were landless and dependent on manual casual labour.

recall.q: What was the mechanism in Anderson (2011)?
recall.a: A breakdown of trade in irrigation water across caste lines.

recall.q: How many applications and advertisements did Thorat and Attewell use?
recall.a: 4,808 applications to 548 advertisements.

recall.q: What did Iyer, Khanna and Varshney find about the SC share of enterprises?
recall.a: SCs owned far fewer enterprises than their share, and the 2005 share was the same as 1990.

recall.q: Give one strength and one limit of correspondence studies.
recall.a: A clean comparison with real employers; they measure only the first hiring stage.

sections.title: Counting caste: data and its limits
sections.big_idea: Each caste data source records different categories at different levels. **Pick the source for the question**, and treat every statistic as a lower bound.
in_plain_words: Census 2011 counts SC and ST only, SECC caste data was never released, NFHS, PLFS and HCES give broad categories, IHDS adds practice questions, and Bihar 2023 counted every caste in one state. Census 2027 will include caste, with a reference date of 1 March 2027 and 40 notified questions.

Between 2001 and 2011 the SC population grew 20.8% and the ST 23.7%. The SECC's open-ended caste column produced over 46 lakh names. Code caste by asking religion first, then category, optionally jati with consent, recording the state list and allowing 'prefer not to say'. Disaggregate, since an overall 62% can hide a 30-point gap.

Reporting outcomes by caste category, and caste with sex where samples allow.

worked_example.title: Read the illustrative gaps
worked_example.setup: The deck's illustrative table: enrolled in scheme (%) Others 71, SC 48, ST 41; received full benefit Others 64, ST 33; turned away ST 21, Others 4.
steps: Enrolment gap between Others and STs = 71 − 41 = 30 points.
Full-benefit gap = 64 − 33 = 31 points.

worked_example.answer: Gaps of 30, 31 and 17 points that an overall average conceals.

Collecting caste as free text with no code list. The SECC recorded 4,28,677 castes in Maharashtra against 494 official entries.
Inferring caste from surnames or asking in front of neighbours.
Reading changes over time without noting that lists changed.

recall.q: Which source gives caste detail for every caste in one state?
recall.a: The Bihar survey 2023.

recall.q: What is the Census 2027 reference date?
recall.a: 00:00 hours on 1 March 2027.

recall.q: How much did SC and ST populations grow from 2001 to 2011?
What are the five steps of the coding protocol?
recall.a: Ask religion, ask category, optionally ask jati, record the state list, allow 'prefer not to say'.

recall.q: Name two limits of caste data.
recall.a: Any two of aggregation, legal definitions, reporting, change over time, missing jati.

sections.title: Beyond Hindu India and beyond India
sections.big_idea: Caste crosses religions and borders, and each country answers it with different law. **Treat official counts as lower bounds** where the law omits groups.
in_plain_words: Dalits who became Christians, Muslims, Sikhs or Buddhists carried caste with them. Paragraph 3 of the 1950 Order limits SC status to Hindus, Sikhs and Buddhists, so Christian and Muslim Dalits are outside it. Ghazi Saaduddin has been pending since 2004, and the Balakrishnan Commission report was ready by June 2026 but not public.

Nepal's Muluki Ain of 1854 codified caste, and the 2011 Act and 2015 Constitution forbid it, yet violence continues. Pakistan counted Scheduled Castes separately in 2017, at 0.41%. Bangladesh's 2022 bill was not enacted. Sri Lanka's 1957 Act reverses the burden of proof. Strong law is a starting point, and enforcement is still to follow.

key_terms.meaning: Nepal's 1854 National Code placing every group in a legal caste hierarchy.
Part of the 1950 Order limiting SC status to Hindus, Sikhs and Buddhists.
Appointed 6 October 2022 to examine SC status for Dalit converts.
A census religion category in 2017, counted separately from Hindus.
The accused must prove the disability was not imposed because of caste.

worked_example.title: Check the Nepal and Pakistan figures
worked_example.setup: Nepal's Dalit population is 3,898,990 of 29,164,578 people, with Hill 8.6% and Madheshi 4.8%. Pakistan's Hindus are 1.73% and Scheduled Castes 0.41%.
steps: Hill plus Madheshi = 8.6 + 4.8 = 13.4, which matches.
Pakistan's closest guide to its Dalit population adds the two figures: 1.73 + 0.41 = 2.14.
The deck warns 0.41% alone is a lower bound for Dalits.
worked_example.answer: 13.4% in Nepal, and 2.14% as the combined Pakistan guide.

mistakes: Reading 'Are you SC?' as counting all Dalits. Christian and Muslim Dalits are outside the SC list.
Citing Bangladesh's Anti-Discrimination Bill as law. It had not passed.
Treating Nepal's strong law as effective. Commentary calls the 2011 Act ineffective in practice.
Using Pakistan's 0.41% as the Dalit total, when Dalits who chose 'Hindu' are outside it.

recall.q: Which faiths' Dalits can hold SC status?
recall.a: Hindu, Sikh and Buddhist.

recall.q: Which case challenging the Order has been pending since 2004?
recall.a: Ghazi Saaduddin v State of Maharashtra.

recall.q: What did Nepal's Muluki Ain do in 1854?
recall.a: Placed every group in a legal caste hierarchy.

recall.q: What is Sri Lanka's distinctive feature?
recall.a: A reverse burden of proof on caste motive under Section 2(4).

recall.q: What share of Nepal's population is Dalit?

sections.title: Working on caste in programmes and research
sections.big_idea: Use a design checklist, a targeting decision table and ethical data practice. **Plan who asks, who is asked and what is recorded.**
in_plain_words: The checklist runs: context, access, targeting, staffing, risk and measurement. The decision table matches situations to approaches: direct SC targeting where untouchability bars access, targeting within categories for captured benefits, universal design with disaggregated monitoring for uneven uptake, separate groups in dominant-caste villages, and name-blind screening for hiring.

Collect caste data with consent, minimum detail, separate storage and no identifying small-area tables, noting the DPDP duties from 13 May 2027. The caste of enumerators shapes answers, so use mixed teams. Organisations reproduce caste patterns too. Write precisely: state the group, the figure, the source and the date, and use consent-based images or none.

key_terms.meaning: Asks about assets, networks, segregation, violence and dignity, with outcomes disaggregated.
Removing names from applications at partner employers.
A separate hamlet, as in the 110 SC households 600 metres away.
Collect category only, unless jati is needed for a stated analysis.
Enumerators of different castes, with matching for sensitive questions.

worked_example.title: Place the pumps
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a village of 400 households has 260 dominant OBC households, 110 SC households in a tola and 30 others. The panchayat proposes four pumps, all in the main settlement.
steps: Check the total: 260 + 110 + 30 = 400 households.
A proportional share of the four pumps = 4 × 0.275 = 1.1.
The deck's design puts at least one pump in the SC tola, with a women's committee including SC members.
worked_example.answer: About one pump for the SC tola, and monitoring that records who draws water and any refusal.

mistakes: Reporting average distance to water, which hides the SC tola.
Letting officials from the dominant caste prepare and verify beneficiary lists.
Having enumerators skip the Dalit tola because it is far or 'unsafe'.
Writing 'Upliftment of Dalits' when the evidence is a change in access for SC households.

recall.q: Name the six stages of the design checklist.
recall.a: Context, access, targeting, staffing, risk, measurement.

recall.q: What targeting approach fits untouchability-driven exclusion?
recall.a: Target SC hamlets and households directly.

recall.q: What does the DPDP research exemption cover?
recall.a: Processing for research, archiving or statistical purposes where data is not used to decide about an individual.

recall.q: Why do enumerators' castes matter?
recall.a: They affect what respondents say and who agrees to take part.

recall.q: What does safeguarding need to cover?
recall.a: Caste harm, including a safe channel in the anti-harassment policy.

sections.title: Movements, open questions and where next
sections.big_idea: Dalit and Adivasi movements built the legal and political terrain. **Five open questions** will shape programmes and data for years.
in_plain_words: Dalit politics moved from civic rights at Mahad (1927) to religious exit at Nagpur (1956), cultural assertion with the Dalit Panthers (1972), electoral power with the BSP (1984) and defence of the PoA Act after Mahajan (2018). Adivasi movements run from the Santhal Hul on 30 June 1855 to PESA and the Forest Rights Act.

Open questions as of October 2026 include how Census 2027 codes caste, state sub-classification after Davinder Singh, SC status for Dalit Christians and Muslims, what follows Article 334 in 2030, and the 50% ceiling. The summary ties the course together: caste is a structure, jati matters in the field, and data should be collected with consent. Return to the three questions.

key_terms.meaning: Group formed in Bombay in 1972 by young writers, including Namdeo Dhasal.
The 1855 Adivasi rebellion under Sidho and Kanho Murmu.
Extends Part IX to Scheduled Areas; gram sabha powers over forest produce and land.
Recognises individual and community forest rights through the gram sabha.
Ends political reservation eighty years after commencement, in January 2030, unless amended.

worked_example.title: Date the Article 334 deadline
worked_example.setup: The deck says Article 334 ends political reservation eighty years from the commencement of the Constitution in 1950, unless Parliament amends it.
steps: Deadline year = 1950 + 80 = 2030.
The deck gives the date as January 2030.
The open question is what follows, and the thing to watch is a constitutional amendment before January 2030.
Track it through primary sources: gazettes, judgments and Census releases.
worked_example.answer: The deadline is January 2030, so watch for an amendment before then.

mistakes: Treating Dalit and Adivasi struggles as one. The deck says STs are a constitutional category distinct from caste, though they share exclusion from land and services.
Citing the Balakrishnan report as published. It had not been made public in the sources checked as of October 2026.
Treating Census 2027's caste coding as settled. The coding scheme has not been published.
Working on caste without the movements. Partnering with them brings legitimacy and local knowledge.

recall.q: What happened at Mahad on 20 March 1927?
recall.a: Ambedkar led a satyagraha to drink from the public Chavdar tank.

recall.q: When was the BSP founded?
recall.a: 14 April 1984, by Kanshi Ram.

recall.q: What are two open questions listed?
recall.a: Any two of Census 2027 coding, state sub-classification, SC status for Dalit Christians and Muslims, Article 334 in 2030, the 50% ceiling.

recall.q: Which law extends Part IX to Scheduled Areas?
recall.a: PESA, 24 December 1996.

recall.q: Which course does the deck recommend first if you work directly with Dalit and Adivasi communities?
recall.a: Social Margins 101.

notes.2: The agenda groups the course into ideas and history (Sections 2 to 4), law (5 and 6), economics and data (7 and 8), region (9) and practice (10 and 11). Use it to jump to what you need. For programme design, read **Section 1 and then Section 10** first.
notes.4: Compare the two lenses. Treating caste as culture leaves a programme 'neutral' and puts differences in uptake down to awareness. Treating it as structure asks who is excluded, by whom and through which institution. The course takes the structural view, and the examples (land, interviews, septic tanks, panchayats) are **questions with caste answers**.
notes.5: Learn the 2011 figures: Scheduled Castes at 201.4 million (16.6%) and Scheduled Tribes at 104.3 million (8.6%), together a quarter of the population. They are legal categories, so counts follow notified lists. Note the missing group: OBCs have **no Census count since 1931**, which is why the Bihar survey and Census 2027 matter.
notes.6: Use the three questions at design, delivery and evaluation: who is in the data, who controls the access point, who benefits when measured separately. Each row pairs a question with a field example. The self-help group in an upper-caste courtyard is worth remembering, because **the venue itself can exclude**.
notes.7: Poverty targeting alone misses caste. The slide's evidence is that Dalit graduates with the same qualifications get fewer interview calls, and SC and ST entrepreneurs own far fewer enterprises than their population share. The caste-aware lens **disaggregates every outcome** and treats social exclusion as a cause of poverty in its own right.
notes.8: Use the legal category when you mean the legal category and the self-chosen name for people and movements. Note the contrast between Scheduled Castes (Article 341) and Dalit (a self-chosen name, taken up by the Dalit Panthers in 1972). One field rule matters most: **never write a person's caste into a report without consent and need**.
notes.9: This slide is your reading route: ideas and history in Sections 2 to 4, law, economics and data in 5 to 8, region in 9, practice in 10 and 11. Dates and legal positions are stated as of October 2026, so **check for later judgments** before relying on any slide in court.
notes.11: Keep varna and jati apart. Varna is a four-part scheme from Brahmanical texts, written down by priests. Jati is the endogamous birth group people actually belong to, in the thousands and regional. The slide's test is 1,241 notified SC groups: no four-part scheme can describe that, so **work with jati**.
notes.12: Ambedkar's 1916 argument is that endogamy is the defining feature of caste: marrying inside the jati reproduces the group. Occupation, rank and food rules vary by region, and this rule keeps boundaries closed. About 5% of marriages being inter-caste (IHDS-II) shows how well **assets, networks and status stay inside groups**.
notes.13: Read the table as a map of where a programme meets caste. Endogamy shows up in dowry and honour violence, hierarchy at a training lunch, hereditary occupation in sanitation, purity and pollution in separate cups, and segregation in where a tap or anganwadi is placed. **Ask which feature is active** where you work.
notes.14: Untouchability is the extreme form. The IHDS-II test counted a household if it said yes to practising it or no to letting an SC person into the kitchen: 27% overall, 52% among Brahmin respondents and 33% among OBC. Self-reports probably understate it, because **admitting it means admitting an offence**.
notes.15: Averages hide a wide spread: admitted practice was highest in the Hindi-speaking north and centre and lowest in West Bengal and Kerala. The telling figures are within groups that are themselves discriminated against: 15% of SC and 22% of ST respondents admitted it, which shows **how entrenched graded hierarchy is**.
notes.16: Ambedkar's phrase is 'graded inequality': every group has someone below it, which gives most groups a stake in the order and makes solidarity hard. Two practical lessons follow. A Dalit group is rarely homogeneous, as the 2024 judgment shows, so research should **report by jati or at least by SC, ST, OBC and others**.
notes.17: Use the three columns to answer anyone who says caste is disappearing: ask which feature they mean. Hereditary occupation, city food rules and open legal disabilities weakened. Endogamy, land concentration, segregated residence and sanitation work by Dalit castes persisted. Caste associations, parties and online networks **grew**.
notes.19: Every caste category has a history, from colonial 'depressed classes' lists to a 1901 attempt at a national ladder. Use the five-step timeline as a spine: local hierarchies, colonial censuses from 1871, the 1901 ranking, the 1950 lists, and caste enumeration returning in 2027. That history makes you **a more careful user of caste data**.
notes.20: Risley's 1901 census tried to place every Hindu caste under the four varnas by social precedence, and used anthropometry to argue caste was racial, a theory now treated as pseudo-science. The effect was that groups petitioned for higher names. The lesson: **a category on an official form invites people to organise around it**.
notes.21: Dirks argues that census-taking, ethnography and law made caste the master category of colonial governance, creating the thing they claimed to describe. The criticism is that this can underplay untouchability's long precolonial history. Keep both points: **caste predates colonial rule, and colonial rule changed how it was recorded, ranked and used**.
notes.22: Sanskritisation is mobility inside the hierarchy: a group adopts the practices of higher castes to claim higher status, and the hierarchy itself stays unchanged. The gender link is practical. It has often meant withdrawing women from paid work outside the home, which can show up in **labour force data**.
notes.23: A dominant caste is numerically strong locally and holds economic and political power, above all through land, whatever its ritual rank. The delivery lesson is direct: panchayat leaders, input dealers, water sellers and moneylenders often come from it, so a programme routed through local elites **is routed through the dominant caste**.
notes.24: Treat the four lenses as a checklist of mechanisms and skip the contest between them. Each names something real and misses something: purity misses power and land, dominance misses ritual and identity in cities, colonial construction misses precolonial untouchability. The anti-caste critique misses little and is **the most practice-oriented**.
notes.25: The Poona Pact (24 September 1932) swapped separate electorates for reserved seats in a joint electorate. Learn the trade-off in the two boxes: separate electorates give representatives answerable to Dalits, while reserved seats let everyone vote. Articles 330 and 332 adopted the second, and **Section 6 returns to what reserved seats deliver**.
notes.26: Five lessons for a baseline survey: categories are made and lists change, so record the list version; classification is political; local rank varies; counting changes behaviour; and self-identification beats imputation. Guessing from surnames is **error-prone and can be harmful**. Keep these five in mind for the data section.
notes.28: Phule (1827–1890) starts sustained modern anti-caste action. Remember three markers: the 1848 school for lower-caste girls with Savitribai teaching, Gulamgiri and the Satyashodhak Samaj in 1873, and opening his own well to all castes. He **linked caste, gender and education** decades before they became policy categories.
notes.29: Savitribai Phule taught in the 1848 school against fierce resistance, and the Phules supported widow remarriage. The link Ambedkar drew in 1916 is that endogamy requires controlling women. So caste is a **gender system as much as an economic one**, and programmes on early marriage or violence meet it through honour norms.
notes.30: Use the five dates as anchors: 1916 endogamy, 1927 Mahad, 1932 Poona Pact, 1936 Annihilation of Caste, 1956 conversion. The slide calls his analysis the most practical theory of caste because it **names mechanisms that can be changed**. Remember too that he chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly.
notes.31: Annihilation of Caste was an address never delivered: the Lahore reform group asked him to cut it, he refused, the conference was cancelled and he published it himself in 1936. His argument goes further than inter-marriage. People observe caste from religious conviction, so the remedy includes **destroying belief in the sanctity of the Shastras**.
notes.32: Ambedkar's reply to 'caste is a division of labour' is labour economics. Efficiency needs occupations chosen by aptitude and freedom to move, while caste fixes occupation by birth and wastes talent. The Munshi and Rosenzweig result in Section 7 is the modern echo: **networks kept boys on traditional schooling paths**.
notes.33: Ambedkar's positive ideal is liberty, equality and fraternity, with fraternity meaning many shared interests and free contact between groups. Small programme forms are mixed-caste groups on neutral ground and rotated leadership. Heed the caution: forced contact without protection can invite backlash, so **design for safety first**.
notes.34: Phule and Ambedkar belong to a wider tradition, mapped by region in the table: Narayana Guru, Periyar and the Self-Respect Movement, and Kanshi Ram and the BSP. Ambedkar judged the bhakti saints ineffective against caste. For any quotation, **go to a published edition** of the original writing.
notes.35: Turn the analysis into four things to look for. Each row pairs a mechanism with an observable sign and a response: endogamy with violence against couples, occupational assignment with sanitation work, graded inequality with capture inside SC and ST groups, and religious sanction with custom, answered by awareness of **Article 17**.
notes.37: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and makes enforcing a disability from it an offence, one of the few provisions that speaks to private conduct. Two companions: Article 15(2) guarantees access to shops, wells and roads, and Article 46 directs the State to protect weaker sections. Parliament gave Article 17 effect through **two statutes**.
notes.38: The Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955 (first the Untouchability (Offences) Act, renamed in 1976) covers public worship, shops, hospitals, schools and services, and forced scavenging in Section 7A. Offences are cognisable and tried summarily. Note Section 15A, the State's duty to provide **legal aid, special courts and committees**.
notes.39: By the 1980s the PCR Act did not reach the violence that enforces caste, so the PoA Act 1989 defined specific atrocities by a person outside the SC and ST communities against SC or ST persons. The Act applies where the victim is SC or ST **and the accused is not**. Penalties are higher than under the general criminal law.
notes.40: The 2015 amendment widened the law after Dalit and Adivasi organisations showed that common humiliations fell outside the 1989 list. The table gives new offences, exclusive Special Courts, a victims' rights chapter (Section 15A), trial within two months of the charge sheet as far as possible, and presumed knowledge of caste. The 15A rights are **most useful to programme staff**.
notes.41: Follow the timeline. Mahajan (2018) added safeguards for the accused, protests followed, Parliament inserted Section 18A, the Court recalled the Mahajan directions in 2019 and Prathvi Raj Chauhan upheld the amendment in 2020. Section 18A reversed all three safeguards: **no preliminary inquiry, no approval for arrest, no anticipatory bail**.
notes.42: Manual scavenging is the clearest surviving case of caste-assigned work. The 2013 Act replaced a 1993 Act, widened the definition and banned hazardous manual cleaning of sewers and septic tanks. Keep the figures: 58,098 identified, 32,473 in Uttar Pradesh, and **Rs 30 lakh compensation** for a sewer death. Critics call the protective-gear exemption an escape clause.
notes.43: The government separates manual scavenging from hazardous cleaning of sewers and septic tanks, and by that line reports no deaths from the first. It does report deaths from the second: 498 from January 2019 to June 2026. **Check which definition a figure uses** before you quote it.
notes.44: Trace the path from incident to outcome: fear of reprisal, police delay in registering the FIR under the right sections, weak evidence and hostile witnesses, long trials, then acquittal or compromise. Each stage is a place a paralegal or legal-aid partner can help. **Record the dates and sections**, compensation paid and time to charge sheet.
notes.45: Article 338 creates the National Commission for Scheduled Castes, Article 338A (2003) the one for Scheduled Tribes, and Article 338B (2018) gives the OBC commission constitutional status. The practical tip is at the bottom: a complaint to a commission can **move a stalled police case**, so keep copies of every submission.
notes.47: Equal treatment of unequally placed groups would preserve inequality, so the Constitution permits special provisions: 15(4) and 15(5) for admissions, 15(6) for EWS, 16(4) and 16(4A) for posts and promotion, 16(6) for EWS posts up to 10%. Learn the **clause-to-purpose pairing** in the table.
notes.48: Scheduled Caste status is set by notification under Article 341 and changed only by Parliament, so lists are state-specific. Paragraph 3 of the 1950 Order limits SC status to Hindus, Sikhs and Buddhists. For data, that means **surveys asking 'Are you SC?' undercount Dalits of other faiths**. Record the state list and its date.
notes.49: Memorise the central figures for direct recruitment by open competition: 15% SC, 7.5% ST, 27% OBC, plus 10% for economically weaker sections outside those groups. States set their own percentages for state posts. Check the chart with arithmetic: **15 + 7.5 + 27 = 49.5**.
notes.50: The Mandal Commission (1980) identified 3,743 backward castes and communities, estimated 52% of the population and recommended 27% reservation in central posts. The 52% rested on projections from the 1931 Census, the last to count all castes, which is **a central reason for the demand for fresh caste data**.
notes.51: Indra Sawhney (1992) set the rules that still frame reservation: 27% OBC reservation upheld, creamy layer excluded, a 50% ceiling save in extraordinary situations, no reservation in promotion, and backwardness as social and educational. Later changes (16(4A), EWS) are **responses to it**, so read the table as a base layer.
notes.52: The 103rd Amendment (2019) allows up to 10% reservation for economically weaker sections outside SC, ST and OBC. Janhit Abhiyan (2022) upheld it three votes to two. Study both sides. The majority said economic criteria are valid and the excluded groups have their own reservation. The dissent said excluding the most deprived **breaches equality**.
notes.53: Davinder Singh (2024) held six to one that states may sub-classify Scheduled Castes, overruling Chinnaiah (2005). The condition is key: the state must justify it with quantifiable, empirical data on a sub-group's backwardness and inadequate representation. For your work, **disaggregated evidence becomes part of the legal case**.
notes.54: Report this precisely. The holding is sub-classification. Four judges wrote in separate opinions that the State should identify a creamy layer among SCs and STs, and that view is outside the operative order. On 9 August 2024 the Union Cabinet said the Constitution makes no such provision, so as of October 2026 it is **a view the Union has rejected**.
notes.55: Follow the three cases in the table. Indra Sawhney (1992) barred reservation in promotion under 16(4), Nagaraj (2006) required quantifiable data and applied the creamy layer principle, and Jarnail Singh (2018) struck down the data requirement while keeping the creamy layer. Before advising on a roster, **read the latest judgment for the cadre**.
notes.56: Articles 330 and 332 reserve legislature seats for SCs and STs in proportion to population: 84 Lok Sabha seats for SCs and 47 for STs since 2008. Article 334 ends the reservation in January 2030 unless amended. Pande's finding is the policy point: reserved seats **change policy**, raising transfers to the groups they cover.
notes.57: Trace the three steps. The 102nd Amendment (2018) gave the OBC commission constitutional status and added Article 342A, the 2021 Maratha case read it as leaving only the Centre able to notify lists, and the 105th Amendment restored state lists. For data, that is why **OBC status must be recorded against a specific list**.
notes.58: State each side of the reservation debate with evidence. The table pairs five claims with the course's evidence: efficiency claims have little direct support, capture by better-off sub-groups has support for some SC groups, correspondence studies contradict 'caste no longer matters', and Pande supports policy effects. Know **which claims have evidence behind them**.
notes.60: Land brings income, credit, status and power, and caste shaped who received it. The SECC 2011 rural data found 29.97% of rural households landless and dependent on manual casual labour. Before any land programme ask **who held the land before and who will hold the title after**, and whose name is on it.
notes.61: Anderson compares villages dominated by an upper caste with those dominated by a lower agricultural caste. Low-caste households earned more in the latter, because trade in irrigation water breaks down across caste lines. The 45% higher-yield figure is the hook. The implication: **do not assume an open local market** in a village dominated by another caste.
notes.62: Thorat and Attewell sent matched applications, differing only in the name, to 548 job advertisements. A Dalit applicant's odds of an interview call were about two-thirds of a high-caste Hindu's, and a Muslim applicant's about one-third. The applicants were college-educated, so this is **discrimination in the modern formal sector**.
notes.63: A correspondence study holds everything constant except the caste or religion signal, so a callback gap is the employer's response to it. Strengths: a clean comparison, real employers, no reliance on self-reports. Limits: it measures only the first hiring stage, names must signal reliably, and employers do not consent. **Weigh the ethics against the public value**.
notes.64: Iyer, Khanna and Varshney used three Economic Censuses to compare ownership by caste. SCs and STs owned far fewer enterprises than their population share, and OBCs about their share. The line to retain: **the SC share of enterprises in 2005 was the same as in 1990**. Compare population share with ownership share in the chart.
notes.65: The ownership gap was not significantly associated with literacy, schooling or reliance on farming. The table lists five barriers with a lever each: networks, credit, customers, social sanction and starting capital. It is an illustrative pairing, so **test which barrier binds in your context** before choosing a response.
notes.66: Networks both help and trap. Munshi and Rosenzweig found that Mumbai's lower-caste male networks kept boys in local-language schools leading to traditional jobs even as returns to English rose, while girls, outside those networks, switched quickly to English. Map networks **before choosing placement partners**, because they decide who gets work.
notes.67: Hoff and Pandey's experiment with 321 boys in each group found no caste gap in maze performance when caste was hidden and a large gap when it was announced publicly. Their interpretation is expected prejudice. In classrooms and trainings, **avoid publicly marking caste**, since the slide warns it can lower performance.
notes.68: Use this table as an evidence map by market and stage: hiring (Thorat and Attewell), trade (Anderson), ownership (Iyer and others), schooling (Munshi and Rosenzweig; Hoff and Pandey) and politics (Pande). The last column lists gaps, which tells you **what to commission next**. Deshpande's book surveys the economics with national data.
notes.70: Match the source to the question. Census 2011 gives SC and ST at village and ward level with no OBC data. SECC caste data was never released. NFHS, PLFS and HCES give categories without jati. IHDS asks practice questions, Bihar 2023 covers one state, and Census 2027 data is unreleased. **The wrong source** thins out caste analysis.
notes.71: Between 2001 and 2011 the SC population grew 20.8% and the ST 23.7%, faster than the population overall, though the notified lists also changed, so part of the growth reflects additions. Remember the extremes: Punjab has the highest SC share (31.9%), and Lakshadweep (94.8%) and Mizoram (94.4%) the highest ST shares.
notes.72: The SECC collected caste names for every household but never released the caste data. The Centre's 2021 affidavit cited over 46 lakh different caste names, including 4,28,677 in Maharashtra against 494 official entries. The design lesson: free-text caste needs **a tested code list, probes for spelling variants and a plan for synonyms**.
notes.73: Bihar's 2023 survey was a rare full caste count in a large state, with a population over 13 crore. OBCs, split into Backward and Extremely Backward Classes, were more than 63%, and Yadavs at 14.26% were the largest single group. It was a state exercise, **separate from the Census of India**.
notes.74: Caste enumeration returns to the Census after the Cabinet decision of 30 April 2025. Use the table as a timeline: reference date 1 March 2027, houselisting from April to September 2026, population enumeration in February 2027, and 40 questions notified on 14 August 2026 with caste in item 10. As of October 2026 **no data and no coding scheme** have been released.
notes.75: Use the five-step protocol: ask religion first, ask category (SC, ST, OBC, none), optionally ask jati with consent and a code list, record the state whose list applies, and allow 'prefer not to say'. Match NFHS or PLFS wording so you can benchmark. **Never infer caste** from surnames or print it on public lists.
notes.76: Study the illustrative table: overall enrolment of 62% hides 48% for SCs, 41% for STs and 71% for others, a 30-point gap between STs and others. Disaggregation is the minimum, with caste and sex together where samples allow. Plan sample sizes so **subgroup estimates are precise enough to report**.
notes.77: Treat every caste statistic as a lower bound on what you do not know. The five limits: aggregation (OBC combines very different groups), legal definitions (SC counts exclude many Dalits), reporting (low crime counts can mean low reporting), changing lists, and missing jati. **Pair the numbers with qualitative work**.
notes.79: The law recognises caste among converts only in part: Sikh and Buddhist Dalits can hold SC status and Christian and Muslim Dalits cannot, under Paragraph 3 of the 1950 Order. Two commissions have examined it, and Ghazi Saaduddin has been pending since 2004. The Balakrishnan report was ready by June 2026 but **not public as of October 2026**.
notes.80: Nepal's 1854 Muluki Ain put every group in a legal caste hierarchy. The 2015 Constitution now guarantees a right against untouchability (Article 24) and Dalit inclusion (Article 40), and the 2011 Act sets criminal penalties. Dalits are 13.4% of the population, and the Hill and Madheshi shares add up: **8.6 + 4.8 = 13.4**.
notes.81: Nepal's law is strong on paper, yet commentary calls the 2011 Act ineffective in practice, and a January 2025 column noted that caste-based violence continues. Hill and Madheshi Dalits live in different regions with different power structures, so **disaggregate them separately**, which the 2021 Census report makes possible for the first time.
notes.82: Pakistan's 2017 Census counted Scheduled Castes separately from Hindus: 0.41% and 1.73% of the population. A Dalit who identified as Hindu on the form was counted as Hindu, so **0.41% is a lower bound**. Read the census form before using the figure.
notes.83: Bangladesh has Dalit and Harijan communities, and the 2022 Anti-Discrimination Bill lists caste among prohibited grounds. Its status is the point: it had not passed when Parliament dissolved on 6 August 2024, and no later enactment was found as of October 2026. **Do not cite it as law.**
notes.84: Sri Lanka's Prevention of Social Disabilities Act 1957 makes imposing a social disability by reason of caste an offence, with up to three years' imprisonment. The table lists Section 3 disabilities from schools to water to cemeteries. Remember Section 2(4): the court presumes caste was the reason, so **the accused must prove otherwise**.
notes.85: The comparison table shows five different approaches: India with Article 17 and reservations, Nepal with an Act and proportional inclusion, Pakistan with Scheduled Castes in the census, Bangladesh with an unenacted bill, Sri Lanka with a reverse burden of proof. **Strong law is a starting point**, and enforcement is still to follow.
notes.87: Run this six-row checklist at the design stage: context, access, targeting, staffing, risk and measurement, each with a question and evidence to collect. Use it in a workshop and record the answers in the design document so they can be checked at review. Start with **who is dominant** and where services are located.
notes.88: Use the decision table to choose a targeting approach by situation. Untouchability barriers need direct SC hamlet targeting, capture by better-off groups needs within-category targeting, uneven uptake needs universal design plus disaggregated monitoring, dominant-caste villages need separate groups, and hiring needs name-blind screening. **Explain the approach to the community** in plain terms.
notes.89: Work the illustrative village: 400 households, 260 in the dominant OBC settlement, 110 SC households in a tola 600 metres away, 30 others. The panchayat wants all four pumps in the main settlement. With a caste lens at least one goes to the SC tola, and monitoring records **who draws water and any refusal**.
notes.90: Caste data is sensitive, so protect respondents: explain why caste is asked and that answering is optional, collect category only, store caste apart from names, and avoid small-area tables that identify households. The DPDP core duties apply from 13 May 2027, with a research exemption under Section 17(2)(b). **Return results to the community**.
notes.91: The interviewer's caste shapes the answer. Plan mixed-caste teams, interviews in private, training on caste-sensitive conduct and supervisors who handle complaints. Watch for enumerators skipping the Dalit tola, landlords present at interviews, and staff refusing food or water, which **damages trust and may be an offence**.
notes.92: Organisations reproduce the caste patterns around them. Use the table as an internal audit: recruitment, pay and roles, grievances, leadership and partners. The Rohith Vemula example shows that progressive institutions are not exempt. Name **caste discrimination in your anti-harassment policy** and give it a safe channel.
notes.93: Precise, sourced writing protects participants. The table swaps vague or sensational phrasing for specific statements: 'SC households in the sample had lower enrolment (source, year)', 'Members of [group] attacked [group] on [date]'. Replace 'upliftment' with changes in access, and **use consent-based images or none**.
notes.95: Dalit politics moved through five phases, each with an example in the table: civic rights at Mahad (1927), religious exit at Nagpur (1956), cultural assertion with the Dalit Panthers (1972), electoral power with the BSP (1984), and legal and digital campaigns after Mahajan (2018). **Working with movements as partners** brings legitimacy and local knowledge.
notes.96: Adivasi resistance predates independence: the Santhal Hul began on 30 June 1855, and tenancy laws still restrict land transfer in that region. Later movements focused on dams, mines, forest rights and self-governance. Know the two laws in the table, PESA (1996) and the Forest Rights Act (assent 2006), both working **through the gram sabha**.
notes.97: Five open questions come with what to watch: Census 2027 coding, state sub-classification after Davinder Singh, SC status for Dalit Christians and Muslims, what follows Article 334 in 2030, and the 50% ceiling after new data. Follow **primary sources**: gazettes, judgments and Census releases.
notes.98: Use the list as a final audit of what you retained. Each point connects to a design decision, a data choice or a legal duty, so mark any you cannot link to one. The last line sends you back to **the three questions from Section 1** whenever you review a programme.
notes.99: These are the most direct next steps: ten related courses, from Social Margins and Indian Constitution to Survey Design and Causal Inference. Choose by your job, whether law, economics or methods. The slide recommends starting with **Social Margins 101** if you work directly with Dalit and Adivasi communities.
